title: M$^\star$: Every Task Deserves Its Own Memory Harness
claim: A closed-loop system evolves an initial program through evaluation, reflection, mutation and automated checks into a task-optimized final program.
layout: 6 colored panels in a cycle, numbered 0–5, arrows between panels
description: A six-panel diagram arranged as a loop, with each stage in its own color-coded rounded box and a numbered circle. Panel 0, top left, shows the seed memory program as syntax-highlighted Python code split into Instructions, Schema and Logic bands. Panel 1, top right, is the Program Pool: a window icon listing write()/read(), Instructions and Toolkit, beside a ranked list of programs with check/cross marks and score bars. Panel 2 (green) is Evaluate: an agent writes episodes to a database, then reads and is scored on a validation set. Panel 4 (red/orange) is Quality Checks, a vertical chain of exec limits, smoke test, compile and LLM auto-fix. Panel 3 (purple) is Reflect & Mutate: a Reflector turns success and failure cases into a diff patch. Panel 5 (teal), bottom left, is the Task-Optimized Memory, evaluated on a test set. Black triangles mark the flow between panels.
caption: \textbf{System overview of \sysname{}.} Numbered stages show the workflow from seed memory program (0) to final test evaluation (5): population pool (1), task evaluation (2), reflective code evolution (3), and compile/runtime quality checks (4).
abstract: Large language model agents rely on a memory harness to write, organize, retrieve, and use past experience. A harness that works for one task often fails on another, because conversations, embodied planning, and expert reasoning require different storage and retrieval behavior. To address this limitation, we introduce Mstar, a method that automatically discovers task-optimized memory programs through reflective code evolution. Specifically, Mstar operationalizes a memory harness as an executable Python memory program that defines the Schema, Logic, and Instruction, and optimizes these components jointly. We evaluate Mstar on four tasks covering conversation, embodied planning, and specialized reasoning. Our results demonstrate that Mstar improves performance over existing baselines across all evaluated tasks. Furthermore, the evolved memory programs exhibit structurally distinct processing mechanisms for each evaluated domain. These findings suggest that every task benefits from its own memory harness, and that memory-program search provides a concrete way to discover it.
